sections.b: Book 1 of the Histories covers the first eleven weeks. The Rhine legions refuse their oath on 1 January (Histories of Tacitus 1:55), Galba adopts Piso on 10 January (1:18), Otho has Galba and Piso killed on 15 January (1:27, 1:41-43), the Senate votes Otho every honor (1:47), Vitellius's two armies set out for Italy (1:61), and Otho leaves Rome on 14 March (1:90). Josephus sums up the same events in a few lines and says Vespasian paused his war to wait for the outcome (Jewish War 4.9.2).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 1:18; Histories of Tacitus 1:27; Histories of Tacitus 1:47; Histories of Tacitus 1:61; Histories of Tacitus 1:90

sections.b: Tacitus presents Galba as an old man who would not pay the bonus (Histories of Tacitus 1:5), left his court to Vinius, Laco and Icelus (1:6, 1:13), adopted Piso in a storm (1:14-18), and died near the Lake of Curtius (1:41). The three writers who tell his death agree on the place and differ on his last words: Tacitus gives two, Suetonius a cry to the soldiers, Plutarch a call to do their work if it served Rome. Suetonius says he died in his seventy-third year, Josephus counts his reign as seven months and seven days.
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 1:5; Histories of Tacitus 1:14-18; Histories of Tacitus 1:41; Histories of Tacitus 1:49

sections.b: From a friend of Nero turned governor of Lusitania (Histories of Tacitus 1:13), Otho moves to the Guard's camp and the throne (1:21-47), and then governs in the shadow of Vitellius's march (1:71-90). His speeches (1:37-38, 1:83-84) are two of the book's set pieces. Suetonius and Plutarch tell the coup too; they differ on small things such as the number of men at the milestone (1:27).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 1:13; Histories of Tacitus 1:21-47; Histories of Tacitus 1:71-90

sections.b: In Book 1 Vitellius is the commander of the Lower army who is pushed into revolt by Fabius Valens (Histories of Tacitus 1:52), hailed emperor at Colonia Agrippinensis (1:56-57), and sends Valens and Caecina into Italy (1:61). Tacitus says he lay in idle feasting while the soldiers' fire did a commander's work (1:62).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 1:52; Histories of Tacitus 1:56-62

sections.b: Tacitus first names Vespasian at 1:10 as the general running the war in Judea with three legions, whom Nero had chosen, and who had no plan against Galba. At 1:50 he is the man some hoped for and Tacitus says was the only emperor before himself who changed for the better. At 1:76 his Judean army swears Otho's oath. At 1:46 his brother Flavius Sabinus becomes prefect of the city.
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 1:10; Histories of Tacitus 1:46; Histories of Tacitus 1:50; Histories of Tacitus 1:76

sections.b: Tacitus mentions Titus twice in Book 1: as one of the Flavians who raised his career (Histories of Tacitus 1:1), and as the son Vespasian sent to greet Galba (1:10). Josephus adds that Agrippa sailed with him, that Agrippa went on to Rome when they heard of Galba's death, and that Titus sailed back to Syria (Jewish War 4.9.2). Tacitus tells Titus's turning back in Book 2, with a different reason (2:1-2).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 1:1; Histories of Tacitus 1:10

sections.b: Domitian appears only in the preface, as the third Flavian emperor who took Tacitus's career further (Histories of Tacitus 1:1). His part in the year 69 comes in later books.
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 1:1

sections.b: Josephus covers Galba, Otho and Vitellius in a few lines of the Jewish War (4.9.2, 4.9.9) and says Vespasian paused his war, that Titus turned back when he heard Galba was dead, and that Galba reigned seven months and as many days. Tacitus has Vespasian send Titus to Galba (1:10) and the army of Judea swear Otho's oath (1:76), tells Titus's turning back in Book 2 with a different reason (2:1-2), and gives no length for Galba's reign. Through Josephus we can add detail to Tacitus's names: Tiberius Alexander (Histories of Tacitus 1:11), Agrippa (1:10) and Poppaea (1:13).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 1:10; Histories of Tacitus 1:11; Histories of Tacitus 1:13

sections.b: Book 1 is where Tacitus speaks of himself most openly: his debt to the Flavian emperors and his promise of fairness (Histories of Tacitus 1:1), the plan to write about Nerva and Trajan in old age (1:1), and the claim that the age was rich in disasters but not barren of virtue (1:2-3). He also tells his readers when reports differ (1:41) and when a speech may have been written by someone else (1:90).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 1:1; Histories of Tacitus 1:2-3; Histories of Tacitus 1:41; Histories of Tacitus 1:90

sections.b: The Guard is the hinge of Book 1. It is the "city's soldiers" who turned from Nero and expected a bonus from Galba (Histories of Tacitus 1:5). Otho bought it (1:24-25) and its men hailed him at the golden milestone (1:27). It chose its own prefects (1:46). A night alarm brought it to the Palace (1:80-82), and Otho paid each man 5,000 sesterces (1:82). Its prefects in Book 1: Nymphidius Sabinus, Cornelius Laco, then Plotius Firmus and Licinius Proculus.
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 1:5; Histories of Tacitus 1:24-27; Histories of Tacitus 1:46; Histories of Tacitus 1:80-82

sections.b: In Book 1 the Senate hears Galba's speech and Piso's (Histories of Tacitus 1:19), votes Otho every imperial honor the day Galba dies (1:47), hears Otho defend it to the soldiers (1:83-84) and, in the face of Vitellius's march, calls him an enemy and traitor (1:85). Tacitus names several consuls and sets out the arrangements Otho made for the year's consuls (1:77).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 1:19; Histories of Tacitus 1:47; Histories of Tacitus 1:77; Histories of Tacitus 1:85

sections.b: Book 1 shows the army from every side: the Rhine legions numbered and compared (Histories of Tacitus 1:55), auxiliary cohorts such as the Batavians (1:59), the oath (1:55-57), the bonus and the exemption fees (1:5, 1:46), and the Guard and city cohorts at Rome (1:20, 1:80). Tacitus names the units Valens and Caecina led (1:61).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 1:5; Histories of Tacitus 1:46; Histories of Tacitus 1:55-61

sections.b: Book 1 gives Tacitus's fullest run of omens: the storm on the day of Piso's adoption (Histories of Tacitus 1:18), the haruspex Umbricius reading gloomy entrails for Galba (1:27), the astrologers who pushed Otho (1:22), the eagle that led Valens's column (1:62), the statues and the speaking ox (1:86), and the delay over the sacred shields (1:89). Suetonius says Otho ignored unfavorable omens when he pressed for battle.
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 1:18; Histories of Tacitus 1:22; Histories of Tacitus 1:27; Histories of Tacitus 1:62; Histories of Tacitus 1:86; Histories of Tacitus 1:89

sections.b: Tacitus names two grants: Galba's gift of citizenship to the Gauls (Histories of Tacitus 1:8) and Otho's to all the Lingones (1:78). Compare Paul's "I, though, was born to it" (Acts 22:28).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 1:8; Histories of Tacitus 1:78; Acts 22:28

sections.b: Book 1 names the whole chain: legates of the armies (Hordeonius Flaccus, Histories of Tacitus 1:9), procurators (Pompeius Propinquus, 1:12; Trebonius Garutianus, 1:7), a prefect of Egypt (Tiberius Alexander, 1:11), proconsuls (Vipstanus Apronianus, 1:76) and the governor of Syria (Mucianus, 1:10).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 1:7; Histories of Tacitus 1:9; Histories of Tacitus 1:10; Histories of Tacitus 1:11; Histories of Tacitus 1:12

sections.b: In Book 1 the Knights share the Senate's joy at Nero's end (Histories of Tacitus 1:4), govern Egypt (1:11), are made collectors of Nero's gifts (1:20), turn up beside senators to flatter Galba (1:35), and take household jobs from freedmen under Vitellius (1:58).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 1:4; Histories of Tacitus 1:11; Histories of Tacitus 1:20; Histories of Tacitus 1:58

sections.b: Book 1 mentions Judea twice: Vespasian runs the war there with three legions (Histories of Tacitus 1:10), and its army swears Otho's oath (1:76). The fuller story, including Titus and the origin of the Jews, is in Book 5.
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 1:10; Histories of Tacitus 1:76; Histories of Tacitus 5:1-13

sections.b: Book 1 shows Rome in three weeks of crisis: a city that heard the news of its emperors' deaths in the Forum (Histories of Tacitus 1:41), a Senate that flattered every winner (1:45, 1:47, 1:85), a flood of the Tiber and a night riot in the streets (1:80, 1:86). The same city is where Paul's last journey ends and where he stayed with the soldier assigned to guard him (Acts 28:16).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 1:41; Histories of Tacitus 1:45; Histories of Tacitus 1:80; Histories of Tacitus 1:86; Acts 28:16

sections.b: Nero is dead when Book 1 opens, but his name hangs over it: the soldiers who loved his vices (Histories of Tacitus 1:5), the fake Nero in the East (1:2), the cry "Nero Otho" (1:78), the man Otho's friends compared him to (1:13), and Galba's "Keep Nero before your eyes" (1:16). Acts speaks of him only as "Caesar" (Acts 25:11-12).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 1:2; Histories of Tacitus 1:5; Histories of Tacitus 1:16; Histories of Tacitus 1:78; Acts 25:11-12

sections.b: Tacitus calls Augustus, Julius and Nerva "divine" after death (Histories of Tacitus 1:1, 1:15, 1:42). The soldiers carry the emperor's image (1:41, 1:55-56). The Senate gives Otho the name Augustus (1:47). Compare the crowd's cry for Herod Agrippa, "It's a god speaking, not a man!" (Acts 12:22).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 1:1; Histories of Tacitus 1:15; Histories of Tacitus 1:41; Histories of Tacitus 1:47; Acts 12:22

sections.h: Adoption of an heir in Book 1
sections.b: Galba adopts Piso on 10 January (Histories of Tacitus 1:14-19) and explains why: the family of the Julii and Claudii is over and adoption will "find the best man" (1:16). He adopts before the pontiffs would in a private case (1:15) and announces it in the camp "as soldiers do when one picks a comrade" (1:18). Paul's word for what God does is huiothesia (Romans 8:15). See the note at 1:16 for Claude's theory on the contrast.
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 1:14-19; Romans 8:15; Galatians 4:5; Ephesians 1:5

claude.title: Choosing the best, or the lost
claude.body: My theory: Galba's argument that adoption picks the best man (1:16) is the picture Paul's Roman readers would have in mind, and Paul turns it over. God adopts people who were slaves (Romans 8:15) and does so because he wanted to (Ephesians 1:5). Where Galba's choice failed in five days, the Bible says the adoption by God holds.

sections.h: Praying for rulers, and rulers who are made by soldiers
sections.b: Tacitus shows an empire where soldiers make and unmake rulers (Histories of Tacitus 1:4, 1:25, 1:57) and where Romans did not know whether to pray for Otho or Vitellius (1:50). Paul tells Christians to pray "for kings and for all who hold high office" (1 Timothy 2:1-2), and Peter says, "Give honor to the king" (1 Peter 2:17). Both wrote under such rulers.
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 1:4; Histories of Tacitus 1:50; 1 Timothy 2:1-2; 1 Peter 2:13-17; Romans 13:1-7

sections.b: Tacitus says astrologers were "forbidden" and "kept" at Rome (Histories of Tacitus 1:22), and that an astrologer's prediction pushed Otho to the coup. The entrail reader Umbricius warned Galba (1:27). See the topic on Roman omens.
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 1:22; Histories of Tacitus 1:27; Deuteronomy 18:10-12

sections.h: Signs in the sky in Book 1
sections.b: Tacitus counts "signs in the sky and on the earth" among the marks of the age (Histories of Tacitus 1:3), and records thunder on the day of Piso's adoption (1:18). Jesus speaks of "great signs from the sky" before the end (Luke 21:11).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 1:3; Histories of Tacitus 1:18; Luke 21:11; Luke 21:25

sections.h: Agrippa II on the way to Galba
sections.b: Josephus says King Agrippa sailed with Titus to greet Galba and, hearing in Greece that Galba was dead, went on to Rome (Jewish War 4.9.2). Tacitus mentions Titus's trip at 1:10 but not Agrippa there. Acts has "King Agrippa" and Bernice visit Festus (Acts 25:13).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 1:10; Acts 25:13; Acts 26:28

sections.h: Slaves and freedmen in Rome's year of four emperors
sections.b: Tacitus shows slaves and freedmen as a force in the capital: slaves and freedmen turned on masters and patrons under informers (Histories of Tacitus 1:2), freedmen like Icelus and Moschus held great power (1:13, 1:37, 1:87), and war captives were sold (1:68). Acts names "the synagogue called the Freedmen's" (Acts 6:9).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 1:2; Histories of Tacitus 1:13; Histories of Tacitus 1:68; Acts 6:9

sections.b: Calvia Crispinilla is said to have plotted famine for Rome (Histories of Tacitus 1:73), food prices rose with the war (1:89), and the flood of the Tiber left the poor hungry (1:86). Acts speaks of a great famine "in the days of Claudius" (Acts 11:28).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 1:73; Histories of Tacitus 1:86; Histories of Tacitus 1:89; Acts 11:28

sections.h: Egypt under the Knights in Book 1
sections.b: Tacitus says Roman Knights governed Egypt in place of kings because it was rich in grain, hard to reach and restless (Histories of Tacitus 1:11). Its governor then was Tiberius Alexander. The grain ships appear in Acts 27:6.
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 1:11; Acts 27:6; Acts 18:24

sections.b: Tacitus tells the end of Tigellinus briefly (Histories of Tacitus 1:72). Saul and Judas are two cases the Bible tells (1 Samuel 31:4; Matthew 27:5).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 1:72; 1 Samuel 31:4; Matthew 27:5

sections.b: Galba's body lay neglected and was buried by his steward (Histories of Tacitus 1:49), Piso and Vinius by their families (1:47). After Saul's death, men of Jabesh-gilead took his body down and buried it (1 Samuel 31:11-13).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 1:47; Histories of Tacitus 1:49; 1 Samuel 31:11-13

sections.h: Philippi in a list of battles
sections.b: Tacitus names Philippi among the old civil-war battlefields (Histories of Tacitus 1:50). The city's later history as a colony is the setting of Acts 16:12.
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 1:50; Acts 16:12

sections.b: Book 1 shows the empire Paul crossed: Illyricum (Histories of Tacitus 1:9; Romans 15:19), Spain (1:8; Romans 15:24), Achaia (1:23; Acts 18:12) and the Guard (1:5; Philippians 1:13).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 1:5; Histories of Tacitus 1:8; Histories of Tacitus 1:9; Histories of Tacitus 1:23; Romans 15:19; Romans 15:24

sections.b: Tacitus praises the brave deaths of famous men (Histories of Tacitus 1:3) and the loyalty of slaves under torture. Acts shows Stephen's death with a prayer for his killers (Acts 7:59-60).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 1:3; Acts 7:59-60

sections.b: Nero's gifts of 2,200 million sesterces and Galba's attempt to take them back (Histories of Tacitus 1:20), Otho's gifts to the Guard (1:24, 1:82) and the soldiers' bonus (1:5) fill Book 1. Proverbs: "Do not give me poverty or riches" (Proverbs 30:8).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 1:5; Histories of Tacitus 1:20; Histories of Tacitus 1:24; Proverbs 30:8-9

sections.b: Tacitus opens by saying history suffers when writers flatter or hate (Histories of Tacitus 1:1). Proverbs says of flattery: "A man who smooth-talks his neighbor / is spreading a net for his steps" (Proverbs 29:5).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 1:1; Proverbs 29:5; Proverbs 26:28

sections.h: Justice and its failures in Book 1
sections.b: Killing men unheard (Histories of Tacitus 1:6), informers (1:2), sanctuary that did not hold (1:43), and a new ruler's killing of those who claimed a reward (1:44) are four cases. Acts 25:16 gives Rome's own rule that the accused face their accusers.
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 1:2; Histories of Tacitus 1:6; Histories of Tacitus 1:43; Histories of Tacitus 1:44; Acts 25:16

sections.h: Servility and the crowd in Book 1
sections.b: Tacitus ends Book 1 with a crowd that shouts for love of servitude (Histories of Tacitus 1:90). Israel's elders asked for a king like the nations (1 Samuel 8:5).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 1:90; 1 Samuel 8:5

sections.b: Tacitus says oracles marked the throne for Vespasian and his sons (Histories of Tacitus 1:10). Wikipedia reports Josephus read a scriptural prophecy as pointing to Vespasian, Suetonius an Eastern prophecy, and Tacitus agreed it concerned Vespasian and Titus. Christians read the Bible's promised king as Jesus (Matthew 2:2).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 1:10; Matthew 2:2

sections.b: Jesus told his disciples they would hear of wars and rumors of wars and see Jerusalem encircled (Matthew 24:6; Luke 21:20). Tacitus's preface lists wars, revolts and signs in the same decades (Histories of Tacitus 1:2-3), and his Book 1 first names the war in Judea (1:10). See the spec note at 1:2.
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 1:2-3; Histories of Tacitus 1:10; Matthew 24:6-7; Luke 21:20-24

sections.b: Tacitus says "the sea was full of exiles" (Histories of Tacitus 1:2). John says he was "on the island called Patmos because of the word of God" (Revelation 1:9).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 1:2; Revelation 1:9

sections.b: Tacitus names him once in Book 1, as governor of Egypt and "a native of the country" (Histories of Tacitus 1:11). Josephus adds that he followed Cuspius Fadus as procurator of Judea, crucified James and Simon, the sons of Judas the Galilean named in Acts 5:37, and stopped a Jewish riot in Alexandria (Antiquities 20.5.2; Jewish War 2.18.7). Same man as Tacitus's governor: very likely, by name, province and role.
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 1:11; Acts 5:37; Luke 2:2

sections.b: Tacitus gives Mucianus his first portrait at 1:10: governor of Syria with four legions, famous for good and bad luck, a mix of luxury and hard work, who had suspected Claudius's anger and withdrawn into a remote corner of Asia. At 1:76 he has the Syrian legions swear Otho's oath. Luke dates Jesus' birth registration "while Quirinius governed Syria" (Luke 2:2), the same office.
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 1:10; Histories of Tacitus 1:76; Luke 2:2

sections.h: Sabinus made prefect of the city
sections.b: Otho's Guard made Flavius Sabinus prefect of the city, following Nero's choice, and Tacitus says many looked to his brother Vespasian in this (Histories of Tacitus 1:46). Wikipedia's page on Domitian says Sabinus was captured and executed on 19 December 69.
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 1:46

sections.b: Book 1 names the Capitol first at 1:2, among the shames of the age: "the Capitol itself was set on fire by the hands of citizens." Tacitus tells the fire in Book 3. Galba's crowd, Otho's soldiers and Marius Celsus all figure with the Capitol in the Forum scenes (1:33, 1:39, 1:40, 1:47, 1:71).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 1:2; Histories of Tacitus 1:40; Histories of Tacitus 1:47; Histories of Tacitus 1:71

sections.h: The war first named in Book 1
sections.b: Tacitus mentions the Jewish war at 1:10: Vespasian is running it with three legions, Nero having chosen him. At 1:76 his army swears Otho's oath. Josephus says Vespasian put off his attack on Jerusalem to wait for Rome's decision (Jewish War 4.9.2). Jesus' words on Jerusalem encircled by armies are at Luke 21:20-24.
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 1:10; Histories of Tacitus 1:76; Luke 21:20-24

sections.b: Tacitus says Egypt was rich in grain and governed by a Roman Knight (Histories of Tacitus 1:11). Acts has a grain ship out of Alexandria bound for Italy (Acts 27:6) and Apollos, an Alexandrian by birth (Acts 18:24).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 1:11; Acts 27:6; Acts 18:24
